questions.q: Why is a Kubernetes Job a better fit for a training run than a Deployment?
options: A Deployment cannot request GPUs at all
A Deployment is built to run forever and restart on failure, which is the wrong model for work that should execute once and stop
A Job runs faster than a Deployment on identical hardware
Deployments require a separate Kubernetes cluster from Jobs
questions.explain: Deployments are designed for always-running services and restart containers indefinitely. A Job is the run-to-completion primitive, matching a training script that should execute once and then stop.

questions.q: What does setting restartPolicy: Never combined with backoffLimit: 2 achieve on a Kubernetes Job?
options: The job restarts indefinitely regardless of the backoff limit
The job is retried up to a bounded number of attempts and then marked as failed, rather than restarting forever
The job skips scheduling entirely and runs immediately on any node
The job automatically scales to more GPUs on failure
questions.explain: restartPolicy: Never prevents the container from being auto-restarted on crash within the same pod attempt, and backoffLimit caps how many times Kubernetes will retry creating a new pod before marking the Job as failed.

questions.q: What is the difference between a resource 'request' and a resource 'limit' in a Kubernetes pod spec?
options: They are two names for the same configuration value
Requests are what the scheduler guarantees when placing the pod; limits are the hard ceiling the container can't exceed
Limits only apply to GPUs, never to memory or CPU
Requests are enforced at runtime; limits are only used for scheduling
questions.explain: Kubernetes uses requests to decide where to place a pod (guaranteeing that much resource is available) and limits as the hard cap the running container cannot exceed.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how do most research teams end up choosing between Kubernetes and Slurm?
options: They always choose Kubernetes because it's newer
They benchmark both schedulers on their specific workload before deciding
They usually inherit whichever one the organization's infrastructure already runs, rather than choosing from first principles
They always choose Slurm because it's free and open source
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as usually a platform decision made at the organizational level, not something a research team chooses fresh -- Kubernetes often wins when research needs to share infrastructure with production services already running there.

questions.q: Why is `kubectl describe job <name>` useful when a job fails for no obvious reason in its logs?
options: It deletes the failed job automatically so it can be resubmitted
It surfaces scheduling-level failures, like not finding a node with a free GPU, that never reach the container's own stdout/stderr
It shows only the container's image name and nothing else
It is identical in output to kubectl logs
questions.explain: kubectl describe shows Kubernetes-level events, including scheduling failures (e.g. insufficient GPU resources) that occur before the container ever starts and thus never appear in its application logs.
